Cubes with embedded electronics such as motors and sensors snap together and communicate without wires, so a child as young as five can build a robot.
Children program those robots on a phone or tablet by dragging and dropping blocks instead of writing code.
Phones are powerful enough for rich play, but mobile games still keep people staring at a small screen.
A handheld lighter with Bluetooth, infrared, accelerometers, and other sensors registers real-world actions, such as an infrared hit on a light puck.
A cloud platform uses the phone to relay game data over the internet, automates play so no human game master is required, and lets players set their own rules.
Open-source software and hardware, developer kits, and downloadable designs let others build games and peripherals, including 3D-printed ones, and the platform hosts third-party developers.
A heads-up display relays real-time stats, health, and teammate locations during play.
Ordinary baby monitors play audio that wakes both parents even when only one will care for the baby, increasing sleep deprivation, stress, and conflict.
A Wi-Fi camera sends audio and video to a smartphone when the baby cries, and that classic monitor mode works without a wristband.

Vibrating wristbands wake one parent at a time, the app assigns the cry from each parent's sleep schedule, a phone alarm takes over if a band has no battery or signal, and each parent can have a morning alarm that does not wake the other.
The alert also works with third-party smart bands, including Sony SmartBand and Android Wear devices.
The product is offered on Kickstarter for $180, then through web stores, and later through large baby retailers.
A huge installed base of room air conditioners is not connected, and the smart products available are thermostats rather than a way to connect those existing units.
A pod connects any remote-controlled window or split air conditioner to the internet so one or many units can be controlled from an app.
The system saves energy without hurting comfort by setting an efficient temperature and by detecting clogged filters, open windows that leak air, and empty rooms.
Algorithms learn the household routine from app use and then run the air conditioner or send a notification, because the user wants the climate to happen rather than to control it like a television.
Pre-orders on the site price the basic kit at $160 and each additional air conditioner at $80.

Security is what people most want from a smart home, but most people who want it do not have it, because apartment installation is complicated, requires permission, and is unaffordable, and traditional systems are over-reactive, obtrusive, and unfit for home decor.
A portable all-in-one unit self-installs in minutes and comes with a camera, a motion detector, and sensors for the home's environment, with the same readings on a phone.
The unit's look can be customized with preloaded themes, the user's own pictures, and an Instagram feed.
The same destination connects and controls other devices, including Nest, a Philips Hue bulb, and a Belkin WeMo switch, and a touchscreen gives local control.
Cloud video recording and media archiving are offered as services on top of the hardware.
Because the device is built on Android, developers can build custom apps for it.
People who lack time or cooking skill, including college students away from home, cannot easily get fresh meals, and microwave meals taste poor and are unhealthy.
Households let much of the fresh food they buy spoil, and unhealthy diets are widespread.
A push-button machine cooks fresh meals from ingredient trays using a storage and delivery mechanism, a safe induction cooktop, and a robotic arm that handles time, temperature, and manipulation.
The Foodie app lets users choose, buy, schedule, and share recipes, follow cooking progress, and read tips from experts and other users.
Chefs can specify recipes step by step and teach the machine their motions by tracing them on a phone.
Customers are sent pre-portioned fresh ingredient trays for each recipe.
A meal is priced around $4, the app is free, the machine retails for $600, and the machine can be rented on a monthly subscription.
Drones have no onboard perception, so they are only as capable as a ground operator, require one operator per drone, and crash when flown close to obstacles.

A platform-agnostic sensor and software suite detects obstacles and changes the flight path to avoid them, even if the operator or a gust drives the drone toward an obstacle, with an adjustable safety distance and sensors that can be swapped for the lighting and environment.
The go-to-market is partnerships with commercial infrastructure-inspection users who want to fly drones now.

Smart lighting is painful to adopt: wired switches need an electrician, cost thousands to install, and cannot be used in apartments or condos, while smart bulbs multiply the cost of one fixture and disable the wall switch.

For about the same price as those alternatives, two magnets snap the device onto a standard switch's screws and it mechanically flips the switch, so the user can still use the switch by hand or turn it on and off from a phone.
The same device can turn lights on when the user approaches home and can run vacation timers that mimic natural behavior.
An optional hub, included at launch, is the base station for this switch and for later products.
An experienced hardware manufacturing partner builds the product.
Distribution starts with a pre-order campaign, then online retail including Amazon and the company site, then brick-and-mortar stores.
Outsourcing circuit-board prototypes means paying a few hundred dollars and waiting about two weeks, then paying and waiting again when the board is wrong or the requirements have changed.
A printer can create a circuit board in the time it takes to get lunch, from software the designer already uses, by laying electrical traces with silver nanoparticle conductive ink.
The printer can make multi-layer boards by sandwiching an insulating material between conductive layers.
The same printer can dispense solder paste and bake the board so components can be added without hand assembly.
Customers can buy replacement ink cartridges and substrates directly from the website.
Designers and machine operators move work through mismatched machine software and shared spreadsheets, which makes prototyping cumbersome.
Manufacturing is spread across multiple factories and engineers who are not in one location.
A cloud client can take control of 3D printers, CNC machines, and water jets, including machines that run from SD cards or USB sticks, and run a job remotely.
Operators can change assembly workflows in the cloud so workers see the current process, and a factory setup can be duplicated to another site.
Enterprises pay a site license of about 200K.

A successful app outgrows a single-node database, and a distributed replacement is hard because teams must combine relational, document, blob, and search systems and then deal with syncing, sharding, scaling, and replication.
The product provides real-time SQL on a distributed cluster, fast relative to traditional systems.
A modern architecture makes the system extremely simple to install, run, and program, including on cloud hosts, on premises, or on consumer PCs.
If a node disappears, the cluster removes it, recreates the missing shards, and keeps serving clients while it heals.
The software is open source and is also sold as an enterprise license.
Standard malaria diagnosis sends patients to a clinic microscope that takes about an hour, costs a day's earnings, and can miss a low-level infection that then keeps spreading.
Magnetic biomarkers in the malaria parasite can be moved so the light through the sample shows both whether infection is present and how large it is.
A reusable reader with a consumable cuvette makes the test inexpensive and fast, and a finger-prick procedure does not require clinical expertise.
A patient record stores an identifier and a score, shows how much treatment to give, and keeps diagnoses over time for follow-up and epidemiology.
Remote clinics cannot use many hospital tools because those tools are expensive or too bulky.
An ultrasound system on an iPad lets a clinician capture, adjust, annotate, and measure images at the point of care.
The clinician can send the image to a more experienced doctor over cellular or Wi-Fi and get advice.
The image stream can be broadcast live to a classroom.
At 14,900 euros the device costs about one third of a regular ultrasound, which is aimed at emergency use.
CE and FDA clearance, expected by the middle of next year, is what allows sales in the United States and Europe.
Web growth scattered information across sites, so people jump site to site and rely on stacks of tabs and single-purpose apps.
Contextual bridges across services require semantic search and recommendations together with new interfaces, so people can move from service to service in one place on the web or on mobile.

A typical retailer takes about a month to change prices, while a leading competitor reprices every 15 minutes, so the retailer cannot make timely decisions across the catalog without giving up profit.
The dashboard can compare a retailer's prices with many competitor websites the retailer chooses.
A pricing strategy can maximize revenue while holding margin dollars, and it can be simulated on past data before it runs, which price matching alone cannot do.
The product is sold as a SaaS subscription billed monthly.
Without regular retina screening, diabetic patients risk eye complications that cause blindness, while ophthalmologist supply is not keeping up.
A convolutional network reads a retina photo and returns a diagnosis within about a minute at accuracy above a typical human reader.
Optician chains, general practitioners, and telemedicine companies can buy a per-image subscription priced below current screening fees.
A glaucoma screening model depends on collecting and annotating a large new set of specialized eye images.
Camera software is hard to ship because local networks misbehave, camera brands do not share one integration, and each new customer still takes heavy setup.
A separate part of the product helps the camera owner connect the camera and keep it connected, so the developer does not handle those network problems.
An app store makes putting software on a camera as easy as putting software on a phone.
The company charges a recurring fee per camera.
Current transit cards hide the remaining credit and the pass expiry, and topping them up requires a trip to a physical place.
The card is connected to the cloud and can be managed and updated from a smartphone over the air, including loading a purchased ticket over NFC.
The card works across existing contactless ticketing systems because it is based on MyFair, the standard those systems already use.
Phones become the sales channel for transit tickets, operators put the card in riders' hands, and the company takes a percentage of the tickets sold.
An open API lets other companies add their own services on the same card.
Patents pending cover the mobile ticket workflow.
Existing hot-water heaters waste water, are hard to set, waste energy, and break because the parts that heat the water get too hot.
Electronic controls heat water instantly through the water's own electrical resistance, with no heating elements or burners, so the heater saves water and energy and is reliable.
An iOS app sets temperature presets, including one that cannot scald, and reports status, usage, and the cost of each gallon.
A utility can cap how much power the heater draws during peak demand.
The heater can be added to an existing hot-water system to augment it, as a distant-tap booster, a tank extender, a turbocharger on a lowered tank setting, or a backup when the main heater fails.
A body-mass sensor recognizes the user and sets the temperature, and a motion sensor starts and stops the water.
Childhood obesity is parents' top concern, but adult weight-loss tools are unsafe for children because they require calorie counting, so families have no safe tool.
A safe clinical pediatric program costs $3,500 and meets on weekday afternoons, so working parents cannot use it.
The company licensed that clinical program and created a mobile, scalable version of it.
Children track red, yellow, and green foods by nutritious value instead of calories, and slowly reduced red-food goals let small diet changes produce weight loss.
If a child picks the avatar, the child is much more likely to pay attention to its advice, and the avatar sends personalized suggestions based on the foods the child eats.
Once a week a coach calls by phone, Skype, or text to give specific feedback and to take the food-police role away from parents, which reduces household tension.
The food tracker is free in order to attract families, text messaging costs $35 a month, and live coaching costs $85 a month.
Scale depends on PR and social media and on health insurers, hospital systems, and schools.
A smartphone can run the audiology test at home, including more advanced tests that follow audiology standards.
The phone can create personalized hearing-enhancement settings and use them to clarify digital audio and the sound around the user.
A dedicated hearing enhancer uses the phone only for initial setup and occasional fine-tuning, so the phone does not have to be carried all day.
A cloud connection lets the user change enhancement settings anywhere, with guidance, instead of going to an audiologist.
Data from many users is used to keep improving the fitting algorithm, and those improvements are sent back to users.
The basic app is free, the premium app with cloud support is five dollars a month, and the dedicated earpiece is a 40-dollar subscription that includes device insurance and service.

The makeup industry charges a premium for color that technology can provide for free, and mass retailers can stock only high-volume shades because volume discounts set the price, so niche colors stay in expensive prestige stores.
A proprietary desktop printer works like an inkjet, needs no new software, and prints a wearable color cosmetic from a hex code copied with a color picker in ordinary software.
The printer will retail for about $300 at first, and the ink and substrates will be commodity-priced.
The first customers are girls ages 13 to 21 who have not formed makeup habits yet and who already learn application online, so printing a color is a natural next step.
Raising money pulls CEOs away from executing the company because they must deal with the company, investors, and banks at the same time.
The JOBS Act allows innovations like this platform into the private placement market.
The platform is for growth-stage companies raising between $2 and $25 million, not for startup crowdfunding.
A fundability score compares a company with businesses that have succeeded and failed at raising capital and tells the CEO how to improve the score.
The score is built from the Australian Small Scale Offering Board data set plus other US and global public and private databases.

Investors and issuers join for free, transactions pay a 2% success fee through a broker-dealer, full-service investment banking is another 5%, and an issuer can use a specialty investment bank in its niche.
Online merchants need to confirm that a shopper is who she says she is and then keep her information safe.
The software lets two parties confirm that they hold the same information without ever exchanging it.
A patent protects that comparison software.

Organizations that already hold verified identity attributes can convert them into the format and expose them through an identity exchange so a merchant can rely on a check someone else has already done.
Each verification is charged a fee, and 30% of the fee goes back to the provider of the information.
In most mobile apps the only support options are to leave the app and call, email, or visit a store, and those channels were not designed for mobile.
An in-app agent can see the customer's screen, draw on it, navigate the app, and tap buttons, as if both people were looking at the same device.

The SDK can be added to a mobile app in as few as 10 lines of code, a JavaScript web plugin embeds it in a CRM so desktop agents can help mobile users, and it works mobile-to-web, mobile-to-mobile, and across iOS, Android, and web.
The in-app support technology is patent-pending.
Peer-to-peer delivery keeps real-time session data off the company's servers.
Partnerships with cloud services, app studios, and third-party developer tools distribute the SDK through products clients already use.
The first 30 days are free, then the price is a flat $1,000 a month including 50,000 minutes, with lower pricing for startups that have raised less than $2 million.
The device has the computing power of a mainstream PC and can run office software, CAD, and PC games at mid-range performance.
Inexpensive docking stations replace multiple PCs and gaming consoles and eliminate extra software licenses.

Bulky connectors, the fan, and the heatsink are moved into the dock and the motherboard is miniaturized into the small PC, which makes it fanless, ventless, about 200 grams, and about ten times as powerful as other devices that size.
Patent-pending protection covers outsourcing cooling to the dock.
The owner can upgrade the PC by opening two screws and adding standard off-the-shelf memory and storage.
A relationship with a top-10 ODM is how the company will deliver a reliable product in volume.
Large retailers, including Best Buy and Amazon, will distribute the product.
For enterprise bring-your-own-device use, the PC can bring total cost of ownership below that of virtual desktops.
Booking separate on-demand services for household chores takes time, coordination, and mental energy that a busy person does not want to spend.
The product sits on top of those on-demand and local services, anticipates the need, and uses a real person to coordinate across them in the background.
Vetted local workers do well-paid work they are proud of, visit a customer and nearby neighbors on a set day each week, and group those chores so the economies of scale can be passed on.
The weekly household service is offered at $99 a month.
Partnerships with buildings turn on a whole neighborhood at once and make the service scalable.
It is very hard to describe a visual product in words, and ordinary search returns unrelated results.
A learning mechanism personalizes items from the shopper's search context, location, age, taste, and environment, and artificial intelligence chooses the next question to ask.
Product data is scraped from websites and stores, each item is given a unique fingerprint, and an ontology gives brands and retailers a common language.

Nine integrated sensors and analytics track 33 health metrics in 60 seconds, as simply as a digital thermometer, and can send them to a mobile device over Bluetooth or to a 3G Wi-Fi sanitizing cradle.
Analytic software can identify abnormalities and alert a care facility.

Beyond elderly care, the product is aimed at chronic-disease companies where states and Medicare pay for remote monitoring, at hospitals focused on preventing 30-day readmissions under the Affordable Care Act, and at consumers.
The company makes money from subscriptions, OEM and licensing revenue, and eventually data mining.
Charter captains have no proper way to market their businesses, and their websites look outdated.
The company provides customer service seven days a week.
Every captain is verified, and each captain is interviewed.
Email is the most important activity on a smartphone and takes about 40 percent of phone time.
Reading email on a phone means scrolling through frustrating formats, metadata, and repeating signatures.
A content-parsing engine reformats email into a conversation view so people can mail like text messaging.
Users can mention someone in a message to assign that person a task.
The product pushes senders to keep emails short enough that recipients will actually read them.
Each email moves directly between the user's mail server and the phone, and the company's cloud does not touch message content.
MailTime is built on open, universal email technology, which gives a better chance to reach more people than a closed network.
The first email account is free, and connecting an additional account costs 99 cents.
Turning a question into an insight requires a data engineer, a data scientist, and programmers, and that pipeline takes weeks and is expensive for a small company.
Company data is fragmented across separate services and sits in silos.
The product connects to a company's services and unifies that data.
Selecting an outcome and clicking predictions automatically finds the factors that influence it and builds the model.
Clicking segments clusters records into groups that behave similarly.
The service is sold as SaaS starting at $1,000 per month, with the price increasing by volume.
Heavy industry has no affordable heat that is also reliable and hot enough to replace fossil flames.
A thermal battery charged with cheap electricity stores heat and delivers on-demand hot gas to existing furnaces, boilers, and kilns in place of fossil fuel.
Where electricity is cheap enough, the installation pays back in about five years while offsetting most of the site's carbon.
A credit score affects what people can do, where they can live, and in some cases where they can work.
On-time positive payment history is the most important component of a credit score.
People must already have credit before they can build it, so many Americans have no score or only subprime credit, and lacking credit is expensive and limiting.
For $3 a month, a user chooses a payment amount and term, those payments are reported to the credit bureaus, and the full amount is returned at the end of the term.
The company uses that payment data internally to offer exclusive lending products.

Freight brokers take days to deliver quotes full of hidden fees and to provide documents or status, they take large margins, and when problems hit they disappear along with the service providers and the shipper's money.
Shippers get transparent access to service providers and can choose them by rating and reliability.
Shipping documents and communication are kept in one place.
A sister site lets service providers onboard, update their pricing, and manage their shipments.
Running a backup generator costs four times grid power and undercuts revenue, while more predictable power would let businesses adapt.
Low-cost Android phones, placed in a proprietary case with a circuit board, become sensors that tell users when power is available in their community.
A user can report a local power problem, such as a downed line, to the power company from the app.
Power companies are the main customers, and they can use the platform to communicate directly with their customers.
Students cannot master a topic without on-demand help, cannot easily find study groups or share knowledge and resources, and students who need extra help fall further behind.
Classmates on the platform discuss school, trade textbooks, build a shared study guide, and use files other students shared for free, including files from earlier semesters.
Any college student can offer on-demand online tutoring sessions and earn money while helping other students.
Growth at a campus starts with a campus founder program and a marketing push on the first day of class, and then students invite their classmates.
A restaurant table is perishable inventory with high fixed costs, and a large share of tables goes unused because restaurants do not manage yield.
ResGuru is a global distribution system that lets restaurants change prices automatically based on demand and supply.
A small business either pays hundreds or thousands of dollars for crowdsourced branding or settles for low-quality branding done on its own.
A learning system uses design rules to study a business and design its brand, putting an in-house designer in reach for 50 bucks.
Taylor is an ongoing service that keeps designing what the company needs later, including offline pieces and online assets such as a website, an app, and social pages.
Using the brands it designs, the system can derive brand insights and trend insights and give them to the customer.
Technology in a car goes obsolete, replacing it means buying a new car, and Apple and Google systems in new cars leave more than a billion vehicles already on the road unaddressed.
The consumer hardware is a basic device or a complete device, each priced at $149.99, and the complete device adds Bluetooth, LTE, a Wi-Fi hotspot, and advanced crash reporting.

First-party apps ship with the device so people can use it immediately, spanning teen-driving alerts, crash detection, theft location, repair bids, insurance savings, recorded and social drives, a home link, and Google Glass.
A company can put the devices in its fleet, run business apps such as fleet tracking, customize them, and pay $149.99 per year with the device and data plan included.
Developers generally cannot build car applications without considerable investment, and where they can, the work stays tied to one manufacturer's make and model.
Developers can build connected-car applications for any make and model because the car is reduced to a simple API call.
Developers can add their own hardware by plugging it into the device with backpack technology or by connecting it wirelessly.
Each use of the bottle records when the cap opens and closes and how much medication was removed, and that record is compared with the patient's dosage schedule.
If a dose is missed, the bottle lights and chimes and the patient gets an automated phone or text alert.
The battery lasts through a standard 30-day prescription without charging, and a longer prescription needs only an overnight charge.
Reminder messages also ask why a dose was missed and can alert a clinician in real time, including a recommendation such as anti-nausea treatment.
Specialty pharmaceutical companies pay for the bottle because better adherence increases their refills and revenue, and patients receive it free from the specialty pharmacy for high-cost drugs.
Diabetes care is inadequate because manual logging is tedious, existing digital tools are often incompatible and hard to use, and no platform connects patients to a support network.
A smart cable connects most existing glucometers, including those in emerging markets, to smart devices through the audio jack, so users do not have to buy a new meter.
The app records glucose readings with context such as meals, medication, mood, and food, flags out-of-range values, and can send interpretable graphs to a doctor.
A partner can view the patient's readings from another device, send encouragement, and get an alert if the patient does not sync or test or if readings are out of range.
The platform lets other parties interact with the patient, including insurers offering flexible premiums and pharmacies offering targeted marketing or monetary rewards.
Robots are now constrained by expensive hardware, after brains, sensors, and software became cheaper and easier to obtain.
Servo, joint, and link modules form a reusable set that can be assembled into many kinds of robots and then taken apart.
Combining the encoder, motor, transmission, and bearings into one integrated joint cuts the cost of an industrial equivalent to about one tenth and improves compactness and weight.
A phone app programs the hardware on the fly, records keyframes, and repeats sequences wirelessly.
A browser builder lets users assemble, program, and simulate a robot in a physics engine, share it, and order it.
Sudden infant death syndrome is the leading cause of infant death and keeps parents up at night, and current monitors do not tell parents whether the baby is breathing.
A wireless smart sock sends an infant's heart rate and oxygen to a parent's smartphone and alerts them in an emergency.
Home readings can supply the infant heart-rate and oxygen record that has not existed after hospital discharge and could support predictions from a common cold to a life-threatening event.
Seniors are injured when they forget to brake before sitting or when a walker runs away on a steep ramp, and those falls are costly and often lasting.
Pressure sensors, accelerometers, and encoders apply the brakes automatically when a senior sits or goes down a ramp, and the user can release the brakes to move.
The technology is licensed to walker manufacturers, who integrate it into walkers as they leave the factory.
Shoppers cannot reliably find a fashion item by translating an image into search words.
From a photo, the app finds the same fashion item, suggests similar ones, and can narrow the results by brand or price.
If automated search fails, a human stylist searches for the item and sends links the shopper can buy.
Users can follow other people and shop the items those people are searching for.
The company earns an affiliate commission of 6 percent on sales.
Most websites have no API, creating one is complex, and web data therefore stays with organizations that can hire developers.
Someone who is not a developer can turn a web page into a table and a live API in minutes by showing examples, and can combine many of those APIs into one call.
A free version of the tool will remain available.
A Chrome extension gives anyone a library of prebuilt APIs and extracts that site's data into a table or a live feed.
Bicycle theft is a huge worldwide cost, and existing keyless locks and tracking devices have not been integrated.
The lock detects tampering, sounds an alarm, and alerts the owner.
A GPS tracker locates the lock if the bicycle is stolen.
The lock uses a keyless mechanism.
Owners can share a bicycle or rent it out through the lock, without separate connected infrastructure.
Current voice controls do not work with the popular apps people use most, and they limit themselves to only a few apps.
The app lets a person speak to many popular phone apps from inside one app.
An API hub lets a new app be integrated with a few lines of code so it can be used by voice.
Business products with an API can sell voice access in an enterprise store, and the company receives 20 percent of the price.
Designers can open a store and sell professional 3D-printable files instead of giving them away, and buyers can purchase and download those files to print at home.
Buyers can order a physical print from a network of competing 3D print shops, for local pickup or shipping, and the company profits from the print.
Buyers who do not see what they want can work directly with designers to create new products.

Ninety-five percent of retail sales still come from brick-and-mortar stores, but shoppers get none of the personalized data they get online, and brands see anonymous transactions with no personality behind them.
The point-of-sale system can recognize a shopper at checkout and send a receipt that includes recommended products and rich visuals.
A visual dashboard lets brands see how sales are doing and what they can do about it, including which customers drive growth or decline and what each customer has bought and is likely to buy.
The starting market is standalone mid-to-high luxury fashion brands such as Hugo Boss and Kate Spade, not mass merchandisers, because those brands care about the customer experience.

Mobile application development is hard, expensive, and slow because it requires many languages, technologies, and frameworks, an average app costs $27,000, a simple app costs 4 to 10, and it takes three months before anything is visible.
A non-technical user can drag and drop a library of components and build a mobile app that has the simplicity of templates but can be customized in every way.
The apps that are built are native, which gives users the best look, feel, and performance.
A preview app lets the builder test and interact with the application live on their own mobile device while building it.

WorkSpot reaches corporate apps through existing authentication and the top SSL VPN providers, including Cisco, Juniper, Dell, and F5, so IT installs no new data-center boxes and is running in minutes.
WorkSpot can launch native apps, such as a collaboration session, from inside the work container.
The product collects end-user activity in the work context, including apps used, response time, documents and pages downloaded, and wireless networks.
Insights uses that activity data to improve the user experience and to detect problems before they become serious.
Events uses that activity data for audit and compliance.
Access and control are given away free, and the company charges for end-user activity data instead.

HR is only 20% strategic, such as who you hire and the culture you create, and 80% administrative, such as paperwork and enrolling a new employee in payroll, medical insurance, dental insurance, and 401k.
Insurance brokers earn commissions they are legally barred from rebating, so the company gives clients the HR services and software they would otherwise pay for and is paid by those commissions.

Companies that already have payroll and benefits can connect those systems without re-enrolling or switching, and the payroll connection imports data in about 30 seconds and pushes new employees and benefit deductions back.

Adding health insurance means becoming broker of record with the carrier, policy number, and a signature, after which the company can manage the plan and collect the commission while the customer's plans, pricing, and insurance cards stay the same.

Hiring is a few inputs, after which the system generates an offer letter and IP assignment from the client's templates, collects payroll, bank, and tax information, verifies immigration eligibility, writes the employee into payroll, and enrolls them in health insurance, 401k, and other benefits.
Companies that do not yet have payroll and benefits can get them set up online, without a dozen trips to a fax machine.
A customer can call many local service merchants and still not find one free to take the job, even though qualified small businesses will go out of their way for a new customer.

Within a few clicks a customer names the service, distance, time, minimum rating, and price, Bidzee offers that bid to nearby merchants, and a merchant's acceptance charges the card and schedules both calendars.
Merchants say their current customer-acquisition channels are too expensive, too complicated to set up, too risky, leave them under-monetized, or give them no control over when the customer arrives.
Bidzee connects customers only to verified, rated local businesses, rather than to another consumer as a peer marketplace would.
Good ideas get lost across the desktop, Dropbox, and the inbox, and another file-sharing product is not what is needed.
The system discovers files across email, desktop, and third-party repositories and strips away the file and its formatting so that pages, charts, text, and images can be used on their own.
Each component is indexed and normalized so one search term returns the best page, not the best file, ordered by relevance of both content and context.
The system learns from which content a person reuses after a search, so that content rises for that search term over time.
Natural language processing tells the user what the content is about, so nothing has to be tagged by hand.
Pages from any file format can be mashed into a collage and exported to PowerPoint or PDF without regard to where the pages came from.
A collage can be shared with a person or group as a visual email preview, or saved in the product and opened from anywhere.
Open or free software shares bugs and missing features, support is hard to get, and users and developers are mismatched in knowledge and priority.
A user can pay, and a developer can get paid, directly from an issue page, and many users can fund the same bug or feature.
The company takes a 6% fee for each successful incentive.
Sharing food in homes and underground dinners is widespread and enduring, and it still has to be made accessible to tens of millions more people.
A diner finds a hosted meal online and pays securely, and that payment already includes the company's commission.
Verified hosts have their events protected under a $1 million guarantee.

Public data reflects the real world but is locked in incompatible portals, files, and databases, so people cannot search across it, cannot see connections between sources, and are limited to sources they already know.
A browser plugin highlights companies, people, and locations on an ordinary web page and opens the matching public-data records.
The same public-data infrastructure is launched as a web app and an API for partners.
Commercial real estate marketing, from static floor plans to distorted photos and boring videos, does not show what it would be like to lease the space.
A 3D camera, modified with a digital SLR that controls textures and lighting, captures geometric and photorealistic data from the space.
The end user has total control over navigating the photorealistic 3D model, and every space is streamed on the web and on the iPad.
An end user can edit the model directly, changing time of day and real-time lighting, placing and recoloring furniture, and swapping layouts, and a space can also be shown as it is, empty, or full.
Contract work runs through drafts, approvals, negotiation, and signatures, and representatives juggle many of those contracts at once.
A workflow can show which deals need attention and let people request documents, get approvals, and collect signatures from inside and outside the organization.
Students can place pictures, video, audio, and documents into a project portfolio that other people can search.

Mothers first buy a monthly subscription that includes a reusable sensor and disposable patches, can return the sensor after birth, and later sales scale through referrals and channel partners.

Crowdsourced maternal and fetal data powers cloud machine learning that helps doctors predict and manage pregnancy complications earlier.
Traffic, air pollution, and scooters in Asia that are low quality, out of fashion, and short of take are the problems this e-bike is meant to solve.
The bike is a fully electric clean-energy e-bike.
A removable aluminum-ion battery is more environmentally friendly than lithium-ion, and four packs can go up to 200 km.
High-power Philips LED lights give the rider extended visibility at night, and tail lights embedded in the side give a sleeker, more modern look.
The motor is designed to be more comfortable at startup and to run more smoothly and efficiently.
The frame is made of aluminum-titanium.
A customization system lets the buyer choose the steering wheel, the color, and the components, and additive manufacturing makes those options possible.
The bike is targeted at people who use it for daily community use, who want to replace old-fashioned scooters, and who want to carry them for trips.
The retail price starts at $1,700.
Commercial construction is an unpredictable environment in which water leaks, mold that can grow within 48 hours, and fire damage hit job sites, and most sites have no active fire monitoring.

A real-time end-to-end sensor network built for the job site gives active warning and damage mitigation, logistics data for placing equipment and managing personnel exposure, and a stored record of how the building was built.
Sensors mount with magnets, a hanging strap, or a wrap so they are easy to move on a dynamic job site.
A deployment takes the building floor plan, places sensors through a risk audit, and brings the system live at those locations.
Moving money in Africa is difficult because transaction costs are far higher and settlement can take up to 20 days.
More than 155 mobile-money wallets run in isolation, which makes cross-network, cross-border, and online payments difficult.
The platform supports cash, mobile money, credit and debit cards, bank payments, mobile wallets, and cryptocurrencies.
A split-payment feature lets a payer pay the part they have and invite other people to pay the rest.
Merchants can disperse and dispatch payments to sellers.
The platform can hold money for marketplaces.
Airtime can be topped up to any prepaid mobile phone across 42 African countries.
Transactions are secured by a blockchain ledger.
Transaction processing is easy for unbanked users across currencies.
A blockchain tunneling network secures and interconnects payment channels for cross-network, cross-border, and online payments.
Six patents protect the technology.
The service charges a monthly fee and a transaction fee.

Selling on more than one channel can raise sales by about 190 percent, but multi-channel selling is tedious and time-consuming because merchants must switch platforms and repeat listings, orders, and inventory work, and many merchants still do not do it.
Merchants can connect stores, automatically import products, and publish those listings to another channel, including the extra information that channel requires.
Product data syncs in real time in more than one direction, merchants can choose which product data syncs, and an order updates inventory on other channels so they do not oversell.
The product is an optimized solution for small businesses rather than only for large businesses.
The monthly subscription runs from $40 to $200, in three tiers based on how many products are listed and how many channels are connected.
The service integrates with Shopify, eBay, Etsy, and Amazon.
It targets online merchants that sell across platforms in North America and Europe.
The platform streams mostly local movies, local TV shows, and local music videos.
Viewers can stream the service on a mobile phone and on a TV.
Cloud data is processed in energy-intensive data centers that are under growing pressure from media and AI demand and from rising microchip costs.
Billions of everyday computers and phones sit idle and are unused compute capacity.
Software can put those everyday devices to work on intensive jobs such as video encoding, generative AI, and 3D rendering.
People who contribute a device are paid most of the revenue, up to a stated monthly amount per device, so they have a reason to join.
Customers get computing that is cheaper and faster than the cloud, including large speedups of their workflows.
Putting older devices back to work cuts a substantial amount of energy waste compared with traditional data centers.
Millions of remote sports fans are disconnected from the stadium while they watch.
Fans using connected devices can transmit their energy straight into the stadium.
Fan sound is captured as decibel levels so loudness around the world can be compared with decibel meters in the stadium.
The system captures a unique set of fan data that can feed a team's CRM.
A fan chip that costs $4 plugs into merchandise and makes it connected.
Sponsors get a brand-integration context in which they carry cheers from around the world during memorable moments.
Fans at any game waste time finding food, drinks, restrooms, and each other, and ordinary navigation apps do not solve those problems.
A crowd-sourced social map helps fans find tailgates, parking, food, beer, and their friends.
Fans can buy tickets to sporting events through a Ticketmaster integration.
Genomics, artificial intelligence, and text mining can identify new drug targets and analyze proteins comprehensively enough for a biotech company to make a better and less risky choice.
Researchers who already have compounds can submit them to the platform to find a new therapeutic use.
Pricing depends on how many compounds or targets are analyzed.
Every user action is processed and returned to the site in a 125-millisecond round trip, so each impression is treated as a cohort of one in real time.
Usage-based SaaS pricing lets customers add new items and new parts of a site to personalize.

On a step-down ward, patients may be resting, deteriorating, in trouble out of bed, or already dead, but four-hour wired rounds wake everyone and can miss those changes, and cameras alone do not proactively alert staff.
Video analytics track whether a person in a room is in bed or out of bed.
Medical analytics measure respiration and heart rate from the camera as accurately as a contact medical device, and those vital signs are intended to be a medical device.

Proprietary per-pixel software runs on a normal camera or a low-cost device attached to it, connects to a cloud that monitors performance and pushes updates, and gives the nursing station real-time alerts and optional video.
Patients need to be stepped down from hospitals to cheaper settings such as nursing homes, care homes, and private homes.
Large-audience streaming that relies on a content delivery network introduces about one to two minutes of latency.
Real-time video applications do not scale to enough concurrent viewers.
An optional peer-to-peer Proximity Multicast can further reduce cost, extend scale, and relieve bandwidth constraints.
Video production is split between a tightly controlled studio and agency industry and wild, uncurated user-generated content.
Tools let companies produce high-impact video at scale by engaging their own fans, customers, and employees as filmers, rather than by building a separate creator community.
Terms in the app allow the client to use uploaded video online and in broadcast.
Uploaded video is automatically tagged, analyzed, and processed.
Machine learning lets clients search the collected video by sentiment, object recognition, and transcription.
Clients can assemble a video with online drag-and-drop tools or by taking selected footage into their own editing programs.
Freelance editors can log into the client studio remotely and finish a video within a few days.

Parents of school-going children face five major problems: communication gaps with schools and teachers, the child's safety, security, and health, no instant progress or behaviour reports, having to be physically present to pay fees, and daily needs such as uniforms and stationery.
The app provides two-way notifications and communication between parents and teachers.
Parents receive the child's report card instantly in the app.
GPS tracking lets parents follow the child for security.
Parents can pay school fees online in the app instead of going to the school.
Uniforms and other daily school supplies can be bought in the app and delivered home.
The service is aimed at private mid-high and upper high-end schools.
Indoor carbon dioxide rises to about three times outdoor levels and, at those concentrations, cognitive performance falls sharply.
Most ventilation systems recirculate indoor air and bring in little outside air, because heating, cleaning, and cooling that air uses a lot of energy, so fresh air still has to come from outdoors.
A microfluidic high-density photobioreactor uses LED-lit biochips of chlorella algae to absorb carbon dioxide and produce oxygen more efficiently than trees.
The systems are sold to businesses as custom and standard units, both directly and through HVAC distributors.
Ordinary drinking-water filters do not remove smaller contaminants such as mercury, lead, or salt.
Under-sink reverse osmosis takes hours to install and returns about one gallon for every four gallons put in.
Pressurized reverse osmosis across a semi-permeable membrane removes bacteria, viruses, and lead, and recycling water through four filters before the last one raises recovery to about 80 percent.
A smartphone linked over Wi-Fi can control the purifier, see the dissolved-solids reading, and share it.
Water from the purifier costs about three cents, compared with about sixty cents for bottled water, with an eighty-dollar replacement set and a three-hundred-ninety-nine-dollar device pre-sale.
A parent's only options are to read a child's phone or spot-check activity with saved passwords, and both undermine the child's independence and take too much time.
Machine-learning models trained on public social-network data and users' messages detect cyberbullying, sexting, depression, and suicide risk.
Parents get a text alert when an issue is detected and a weekly email summary when none is found, and they can choose which kinds of issues trigger a notification.
Parents are shown potential problems only, not unrestricted access to a child's messages.
Each kind of detected issue comes with recommended actions tailored to that problem.
Parents can confirm or reject an alert, and that feedback is used to keep improving the detection models.
The service costs nine dollars per month per family, with unlimited children and unlimited connected accounts.
Schools and nonprofits can offer the service through an affiliate payment that supports their fundraising.

Radiologists are overwhelmed because scan volume has grown far faster than reading efficiency, training more radiologists takes too much time and money, and a misread image can seriously harm a patient.
Artificial intelligence helps radiologists find abnormalities in medical images and prioritize which scans to read.
Natural language processing of medical records, used together with the imaging, gives the doctor an advantage in the diagnosis.
The software is integrated into radiology systems vendors already make, so doctors are not asked to adopt an unfamiliar workflow.
The software is also sold directly to hospitals.
Hospital partnerships exchange the software for medical images used to train the models.
Bringing the software into clinical use depends on FDA clearance, which is distinguished from approval.
Most people in these markets are unbanked and lack credit, so they cannot pay online in the usual way, on credit.
Users can pay online in local-currency installments at the company's merchants and at merchants worldwide that accept Bitcoin.
An ID photo and a selfie, together with machine learning on the user's details, social data, outside records, and fraud screening, produce a score used to extend credit.
Repayment appears on a monthly phone statement and is collected from a bank account or in cash at partner merchant locations.
Google ignores a large share of pages on e-commerce, travel, and classified sites, and an ignored page cannot drive traffic or revenue.
Comparing a crawl of the whole site with the traces Google leaves in log files shows which pages were ignored, why, what to change, and whether the results improved.
The analysis is sold to businesses as a monthly subscription.
Connected home devices are easy to hack, and an intruder on the network can reach the household's other devices, files, and personal information.
Once connected, the device automatically lists every device on the home network.
The gateway sends network metadata to the cloud, where threat intelligence and machine-learning models of device behavior block only the anomalous activity and leave the device working.
When one unit blocks a threat, the other units are updated in real time so they can block that same threat.
The device sells for $99 plus $8.99 a month to keep every device on the network protected.
Ordinary encryption makes data unsearchable and unusable, so a software team's core work becomes impossible and the enterprise must choose convenience or security.
Searchable encryption can find encrypted data as easily and quickly as web search without revealing the key, and the search is built on AES-256.
Encrypted Git hosting encrypts source code and still allows search while that code remains encrypted.
Transcranial direct current stimulation can stimulate the brain without surgery.
Priming the motor cortex so that it is more plastic lets an athlete get more out of the same training, neurologically.
Proprietary primer electrodes in a headphone-style wearable deliver that neuropriming during a workout, and a phone app turns the stimulator on.
The technology is defensible because 27 patents have been filed.
The same neurostimulation can help the half of stroke survivors who have a motor disability.
The company sells headsets plus semi-disposable primers and earpads, keeps the app free for now, and may later charge for premium app features.
A large audience wants stand-up comedy, including 91 million people who rank it among their top interests and top comedians with hundreds of millions of social followers.
Streaming has not caught up with comedy, so only about 10 percent of the comedy and 1 percent of the market are available, which is a problem for those fans.
Listeners can search the comedy catalog by artist, by album, and by track.
The service is ad-supported, and seven dollars and ninety-nine cents a month buys ad-free listening, offline play, and exclusive content made for the app.
Transcribing every joke into text powers a profanity filter and radio stations built from the subject of the joke.
Comedians promote the app because they share the revenue from every stream.
The company has distribution with the top record labels and is their primary distribution arm.
Motorists kill a cyclist every six hours, and a pedestrian is killed on U.S. streets every eight minutes.
High-visibility clothing, retro-reflectives, and tail lights are limited and often invisible from outside angles.
Traditional safety vests look like a traffic cone, so safety gear has to be fashionable if people are going to wear it.
Once the garment is illuminated, the wearer is visible on the ride.
Route-tracking software automatically turns on a turn signal and strobes the garment in an intersection so drivers can see where the rider is going.
A brake light automatically flashes a tail light when the rider slows down.
Pace lighting coaches the wearer against a target speed, showing whether they are on pace, too slow, or too fast.
The company's own line is four pieces for the run, bike, and moto activewear markets.
Parents will be able to buy the gear at college bookstores across the U.S. so students are safer at night.
Licensing to existing brands extends the technology into further consumer, industrial, and enterprise uses.
Eighty-nine percent of turnover is soft-skill mismatch rather than hard skills, yet hiring can measure only hard skills such as years of experience listed on a resume.
Cognitive assessments predict job performance better than interviews, work experience, or education, but they are long, expensive, and slow, so no one uses them.
Twenty-minute mobile games distill in-game behavior into a cognitive fingerprint reported as hustle, social, and bandwidth scores.
A model of the employer's top performer, specific to that role and company culture, finds other players likely to perform like them while ignoring gender, education, and race.
Employers pay a one-time setup fee to build the model from their top performers, then a subscription to filter inbound candidates or a sourcing fee for talent already on the platform.
Farms must inspect submerged mooring lines and nets every day, and today that work is done by expensive paired divers whose imprecise paper notes managers have to transcribe for regulators.

The underwater robot is intuitive to pilot, easy to maintain, and a fraction of the cost of existing tools, and it is portable, has replaceable thrusters, a wide-angle gimbal camera, and can hold position in strong currents.
An operator follows an inspection list, stores photos and comments automatically, uploads the record to the cloud in one step, and the farm manager reviews it and files the report in one click.
The same low-cost robot can inspect boats, oil and gas assets, and underwater infrastructure such as dams and bridges.
A developer model lets people hack the underwater robot and use it for research.
Single-serve pods create waste, cost a lot, and are not fresh because the grounds are at least six months old.
Home coffee makers have had very little innovation and use only gravity or pressure.
Centrifugal spinning grinds fresh beans and brews any style from a single espresso at 7,000 rpm to a full filter pot at 2,000 rpm, without disposable pods or filters.
The centrifugal brewing method is patented.
When beans run low, a sensor orders replenishment through a marketplace of local roasters, who receive the shipping and card details and send the beans, so the drinker does not run out.
The company manufactures the machine and makes margin on those machines.
The company takes a cut of every bean order that goes out through the marketplace.
Digital tools available for under $5,000 still cannot cut hard, flat material, so those parts are made by hand.
A desktop waterjet cuts any material from a digital design, more accurately than by hand, and is compact, contained, clean, safe, and quiet, at a price under $4,000.
Four patents are pending on the redesigned water-cutting technology.
Relapse is caused by lack of communication and lack of accountability for recovery activities.
Geolocation and accelerometers check that a scheduled recovery activity lasted and that the person stayed engaged, rather than appearing for only a few minutes.
The support network can see progress dashboards, gets alerts when the recovery program is missed, and can be messaged to reach out when the person starts isolating.
Points earned in active recovery buy rewards such as fitness classes, yoga, and coffee, chosen so they do not trigger a technology addiction.
The first sales channel is inpatient treatment centers, a U.S. market of 3.1 million people per year.
Data the platform gives treatment centers, for referrals, outcomes, and studies, is the path into healthcare providers, insurers, and employee assistance programs.
SQL tables are turned into matrices and executed on thousands of GPU cores instead of the few cores in a CPU.
The system self-configures from the cluster hardware, the data stored, and the team's usage patterns.
The interface is SQL so that analysts, developers, and businesses can use the language they already work in.
The server software deploys to the cloud or to an appropriately configured on-premises rig.
A community edition of the GPU SQL database is free to use for life.

Labor—who is doing what, when, and where—is the vital farm data to digitize, because heavily regulated H2A seasonal labor forces farms to track work to a person and a place, and most farms still record it with pen and paper in a way that fails Department of Labor compliance.
A dashboard app gives farmers and managers a real-time view of the farm with analytics and reporting.
A tablet app in the field captures data that feeds the dashboard, including a quick NFC clock-in and clock-out.
A phone app lets full-time employees clock in and out across locations, and those locations are geotagged.
A labor audit report packages what the Department of Labor requires so a farm can download it and hand it over.
The system calculates hourly pay, piece rate, and overtime, including the rule that the farmer must pay the higher of hourly and piece rate, so payroll stays compliant.
A typical person has many separate online identities, so behavior sits in silos and a single website or app cannot deliver a personalized experience from its own actions.
Actions are not placed in a time context, so a site cannot tell a gift bought weeks ago from the shopper's own upcoming plans.
Brainify ties information from across the web into one robust, dynamic, and encrypted profile of the individual.
The engine weights activities by time so it can judge that person's changing interests and intent right now.
An API lets any company harness that profile and deliver hyper-relevant experiences for every user.
Price is tiered by monthly API-call volume so the service is affordable for every company.

Patients onboard by scanning an insurance card so the carrier supplies their information, then name an emergency contact, choose a primary doctor, and sign a privacy notice instead of a long registration form.
The phone holds a snapshot of the patient's health organized by condition, including medical images, lab results, referrals, and appointments.
Patients keep a message history with the doctor in the case, so they do not have to track everything the doctor says.
A prescription can be sent to a pharmacy for pickup or delivered to the house, and pill reminders can be scheduled from the regimen.
The patient can find a specialist and send the referral to that specialist.
Care is a hybrid of virtual and in-person visits, so the clinic doctor has the virtual context and follow-up after the clinic can be virtual.
Controlling the physician applications, the patient applications, and third-party integrations makes it possible to design an experience traditional providers cannot.
Beyond the company's own clinic, the platform is to be made available to independent practices across the country.
At-home kits measure well-evidenced markers from blood, saliva, or urine, and the current infrastructure can expand that menu beyond 100 tests.
Direct-to-consumer testing is run in compliance with state regulations in the states where the company operates.
Partner labs are CLIA-certified reference laboratories, and their tests are as accurate as a test a doctor would order.
A virtual physician network authorizes the lab requisition when an order is placed.
The company fulfills the kit and manages logistics among its partner labs.
Unstandardized HL7 results from many labs, markers, and tests are translated into the consumer dashboard.
The company does not share the customer's results data.
Kits are sold online from $79 to $399, at a per-test cost below typical out-of-pocket prices and often the same as or lower than insurance.

Custom currency is hard because payment systems are not set up to track every code and interaction, control who can spend it and when, and tie promotional value to gift cards and refunds, so businesses otherwise build it themselves.
Marketing teams get tools to control, send, and track the business's own custom currency.
A simple API integration applies that currency in the merchant's checkout.
The price starts at $90 a month for 1,000 active codes and $15 a month per additional 1,000 codes, so businesses of any size can buy it.
Keeping track of warehouse inventory is a manual, slow, and inaccurate process, so goods are lost, workers spend hours searching, and companies lose money on inventory errors.
The system is built for high-bay selective-rack warehouses with uniform dimensions, palletized goods, and a label on each pallet.
The flying robots fly autonomously indoors to centimeter accuracy without external systems such as GPS, using computer vision and specialized onboard computing.
On-site infrastructure relays the information the robots collect to warehouse workers.
The software tells the worker how to update SAP or fix the inventory error in the warehouse.
Hardware and installation are sold for an upfront setup fee, in the way traditional industrial automation equipment is sold.
The software is sold as a subscription, and data-driven premiums can be added as the system collects more information.
Medical tourism is dominated by travel agents without clinical expertise, which leaves patients with unvetted doctors, poor outcomes, and a lack of trust.
Patients travel for care to save money where U.S. prices are opaque, to avoid waits that can last a year or more, or to reach procedures regulation blocks at home.
Doctors go through vetting led by a U.S. board of physicians, covering credentials, interviews, and sometimes observed surgery, and just 5% of applicants are accepted.
Patients and doctors can communicate in a HIPAA-compliant center by live chat, video conference, and shared medical files.
The company collects documents, records, and payments so doctors can focus on providing care.

Without rapid diagnostics near the patient, outbreaks keep spreading, and current options are either dipsticks too insensitive for early detection or PCR machines that are costly, not portable, and slow.
A vacuum-driven portable chip needs no external pumps, controllers, computers, or valves, so the chip and reader can cost far less than PCR.
Isothermal nucleic acid amplification on the chip has sensitivity comparable to PCR, and the number of lit micro-wells measures pathogen concentration.
An app tracks GPS, patient information, and test results so ministries of health can deploy resources to hotspots.
The first offering is a research toolkit.
Selling the chip as a human diagnostic requires integrating sample preparation.
Selling the chip as a human diagnostic requires FDA clearance.

Most breaches are caused by users, and tools that replace passwords have not been widely adopted because they require teaching the user something new or integrations that need time, money, and a dedicated IT department.
Identity tools that put sensitive information in the cloud create a single point of failure.
After the user approves a login request with a fingerprint on the phone, the phone pushes the username, password, and SMS two-factor token into the browser.
The product works without an integration to the service providers.
An admin can see team logins in real time, ping a device, revoke access, and push an account to a phone at a privilege level that hides the password from the user.
Admins can restrict an account by geography, time, and IP address, and be notified when access is attempted outside the allowed zone.
Admins can change a password in the background immediately or on a company-wide schedule.
The first five users are free, and each additional user is charged a monthly fee.
Product managers cannot see real user needs because feedback, ideas, and backlogs are scattered in tools built for delivery rather than discovery, so teams build features nobody wants.
Integrations bring support tickets, conversations, emails, and interview notes into one place, where an insight can be marked for importance and linked to a feature idea.
Feature ideas are organized by the user need they serve, scored for impact, and prioritized against the team's strategic goals rather than kept as a flat backlog.
The roadmap is generated automatically and can be shared with the underlying insights behind each item.
Chosen features can be pushed to Jira or other engineering delivery systems, and progress comes back in real time.
The system is a hub for the whole company, not only product managers, because everyone at a product company wants to take part in product decisions.
The offer is a per-user subscription starting at $24 a month, reached through content marketing and inside sales.
Talk media such as podcasts and radio are still long and not interactive, so they do not fit mobile-first creators.
The app is a social network where users start bite-sized talk shows on a topic and invite friends or followers to participate.
After a recording, the app reduces background noise, engineers the voice, and can add voice filters and background music.
Creators can share talks on other social platforms and embed them natively on any website.
Brands and top creators can use the same talks to create and distribute audio, not only ordinary users.
Livestock disease creates large economic and public-health losses because outbreaks are caught too late, and a large share of that loss could be prevented by catching them early.
Historic and real-time data can be put in one standard format and combined with genomics on the animal and the disease to give a comprehensive view of animal health.
Livestock veterinarians can diagnose disease more accurately and efficiently at the point of care and can see whether an outbreak may be forming.
Veterinarians can mine records to find the most efficient and most effective treatment for the disease.
The platform lets the pharmaceutical industry find new gene targets and pathogens so drug development is faster.
Customer-vendor relationships between livestock companies and pharmaceutical companies create a network effect that spreads the platform.
Customers pay an annual subscription to access the tools and data, with an added charge for collaborative custom projects.
Traditional gas mowers contribute 5 percent of the U.S. carbon footprint.
Ordinary lawn care means several calls to get a callback, an in-person visit before a price, cash or a check, and a crew that may not show up.
A customer can enter an address for an instant quote, schedule a crew expected to show up, pay by card, and rate the work so only the best crews keep getting jobs.
Human crews cannot clear a backlog from rain, breakdowns, or illness, because the missed jobs cannot be made up with a night shift.
Consumer robotic mowers cost thousands of dollars up front, need a buried perimeter wire, and still do not edge, trim, fertilize, or weed.
The robotic mower mows the yard on its own, turns away from obstacles, stops the blades within a second if it is lifted or tilted, and runs emissions-free on about 11 kilowatt-hours a month.
A technician installs the base, the perimeter wire, and the mower program, and the service then monitors the mower and replaces blades.
The robotic service costs $99 a month, less than a traditional lawn service, and keeps the lawn mowed.
Edging, trimming, and fertilizer can be added for a separate fee using crews already in the field.

People can reach only current contacts who happen to be the right person, or a bot, and bots still cannot handle a real need, so they need a conversation with a capable human they do not already know.
Natural language processing reads the context and intent of a need, and a match-and-dispatch algorithm connects the person with someone at the right time.
Chats are anonymous by default, and contact details are exchanged only when there is trust.
The service is available across messengers, including Kik, Telegram, and text message.
Conversations are indexed in real time so the system gets smarter as more chats happen.
Both people rate each other when a chat ends.
A transactional layer lets a user tip the person they chatted with.
Teams still create decks in PowerPoint, discuss them in email and chat, pass files through cloud drives, break formatting across versions, and need another tool to present or share.
A new format keeps the presentation brief by stacking additional detail under the main slides, so the presenter can open that detail or skip it.
A fully customizable editor changes how teams work together on presentations.
A finished presentation can be presented live with speaker notes, exported for offline presenting, or shared as a link.
An enterprise version puts the product behind the corporate firewall for additional security.

Audits cannot run on every code change, scanner reports are full of false positives that developers stop reading, and firewalls are too permissive to block an attack without blocking legitimate traffic.
Runtime protection inside the application monitors critical functions and blocks unknown vulnerabilities using logic rather than patterns, which is also how false positives are handled.
The exact details of a vulnerability are shown in the interface, as they would be in a debugger.
Installing the protection is no different from adding any other dependency to the application.
The service protects users and customers against account takeovers and brute-force attacks.
Pricing starts at $99 per month and scales with the number of hosts.
Navigation apps pre-compute routes and assume traffic will not change during the drive, so each segment is priced at the departure time and the apps then reroute often.
Loop detectors, traffic cameras, and soon advanced vehicles are more accurate traffic sources than phones.

Time-dependent routing, held as the company's IP, prices each stretch of road by when the vehicle is expected to reach it, and that real-time layer ingests minute-level data, predicts, accounts for accidents, and routes.
Embeddable navigation does not exist, so businesses that move people or things cannot put a real-time turn-by-turn experience inside their own apps.
Integrating the SDK takes five steps and only a few lines of code.
A person is not authenticated by a number, a photo ID card, or a password.
Biometric and behavioral factors can be built into a unique digital fingerprint that authenticates and secures identity.
People choose shoes for style rather than support, so the arch fatigues and hurts, pronation or supination misaligns the body, and the shoes are not comfortable enough.

Prescription orthotics cost about four hundred dollars, take time, are not repeatable, and are corrective rather than comfortable, while off-the-shelf insoles are easy to buy but provide no real support.
The custom insole is available for 75.
Computer vision captures curved foot data from the phone and turns it into something that can be customized.
A proprietary customization engine biomechanically enhances the scan for that person.
A 3D scan becomes a custom 3D-printable file in five seconds, and that conversion runs in the cloud.
The insoles are manufactured on enterprise-grade SLS 3D printers.
The internet-connected toys learn and grow with a child, with the technology inside the toy as the child gets smarter.
The toys come packed with educational content, including jokes, stories, and scavenger hunts, and are meant to stay engaging over weeks and years rather than one-off questions and answers.
Parents get a dashboard of engagement metrics and analysis of how their child actually uses the toy.
Parents can control the toy, including setting a bedtime.
A subscription, plus sales of additional content or features, can move the business off the cyclical toy calendar.
The toy retails for $99.99 and costs about $25 to build at small volume, with a roadmap toward about $15 and stronger margins at scale.
People manage digital life across many apps and have to keep checking a phone for the calendar, cameras, email, and calls, when there should be a nicer way to get that information.
The wall clock's glanceable display shows information in the background as geometric shapes rather than text and numbers.
A cloud platform on the back end integrates services through open APIs.
The cloud analyzes the connected data and decides what information to display, when, and where.
The clock is introduced on Indiegogo at an estimated price of $1.49, with web pre-orders after the campaign and retail after shipping.
High-tech toys are built for boys, while the toys made for girls are not.
Girls ask for friendship and communication, and the bracelets are made from what they say matters.
A mesh network lets the bracelets communicate from device to device, so girls do not need a mobile phone to use and program them.
Friends pair into a color group, and their bracelets glow when they are nearby, brighter as more of the group gathers, and with a rainbow animation when the whole group is together.
Girls can send secret messages by customizing lights and vibrations.
The bracelets are open source, and girls can code custom effects in the Arduino language by connecting a micro-USB port to a computer.
The bracelets are COPA compliant, so girls can communicate with each other safely.
Interchangeable charms and bands are sold separately, and girls can collect and trade limited-edition designs and characters.
